name: ollama

facts.description: Get up and running with Kimi, GLM, MiniMax, DeepSeek, gpt-oss, Qwen, Gemma and other models.

title: Ollama: A Local Inference Engine and Model Serving Runtime for AI
answer: Ollama is an open source runtime, written in Go and published under the MIT licence, for downloading, running and serving large language and multimodal models on your own hardware or through its cloud. It sits at the inference and serving layer of the AI stack, not at training. The one thing to know before adopting it is that it deliberately trades some fine grained control for a very short path from install to a working model endpoint.

sections.body: Ollama is made by Ollama, the company behind the ollama.com site and the ollama/ollama repository on GitHub, and it is distributed under the MIT licence. The code is written in Go, and the project has been active for years, with the most recent push recorded in October 2026. It is not a training framework and not a model itself. It is an inference engine and model serving runtime, which means it takes models that already exist, loads them onto your machine or onto hosted hardware, and exposes them through a local API and command line. In the layered picture of AI work, it belongs above the model weights and below your application: the place where a prompt becomes tokens and tokens become text, images or tool calls. Its model library is the front door, a catalogue that includes Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi, Granite, embedding models and many others, each with a short description of size, context length and intended use.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs Ollama does are inference and serving. You pull a model, run it, and talk to it over a local endpoint, which makes it a natural fit for coding assistants, chat over documents, retrieval augmented generation, agent workflows and safety classification. The blog shows it wired into Continue for autocomplete and chat inside Visual Studio Code and JetBrains, into Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex CLI through compatible APIs, and into OpenJarvis and OpenClaw for personal agents on your own hardware. It is strongest where you want a model on a laptop, a workstation or a small server without standing up a full serving stack, and where privacy or offline operation matters. It also reaches upward through cloud models, which run larger models on datacenter grade hardware, and through a web search API. It is not positioned for large scale distributed training, and the site does not present it as a training tool.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve for basic use is shallow. The site's own framing is get up and running, and the launch command sets up coding tools with local or cloud models without environment variables or config files. A developer who can use a terminal can be running a model in minutes. What takes longer is understanding the trade offs: quantization, context length, memory pressure, GPU versus CPU execution, and how model scheduling behaves on multi GPU systems. The blog notes a significantly improved scheduling system that reduces out of memory crashes and improves GPU utilization, which tells you these are real concerns rather than abstractions. Prerequisites are modest. You need comfort with a command line and some sense of how much memory your hardware has. You do not need mathematics or machine learning theory to serve a model, though that knowledge helps when choosing between a 7B and a 70B model or judging benchmark claims. The official site offers a model library, a blog and integration guides, but it is written for practitioners rather than as a structured course for beginners.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around Ollama is broad and mostly integration shaped. The library spans Meta's Llama family, DeepSeek, Qwen, Google's Gemma, Mistral, Microsoft's Phi, IBM Granite, BAAI's BGE-M3, Snowflake embedding models, LLaVA and others, which means most popular open weights are reachable through one interface. On the tooling side the site documents Continue, Claude Desktop as a third party gateway, Claude Code with subagents and web search, OpenAI's Codex CLI, OpenJarvis, OpenClaw, LanceDB for local retrieval, and Hugging Face tooling for fine tuning. There are partnerships with OpenAI, NVIDIA and ROOST, and support for the Anthropic Messages API. The project reports serving 8.9 million developers and having raised 88 million dollars from Benchmark, Theory Ventures, 8VC, Y Combinator and angel investors. The repository shows a very large star count, which is a rough signal of attention rather than a measure of production use.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Ollama is built for both, but with different emphases. For prototyping it is close to ideal: one command, a local endpoint, and a library of models you can swap without rewriting your application. For production it offers more than a toy, including model scheduling, multi GPU utilization, cloud models on datacenter hardware, per token pricing on paid plans, and privacy terms with zero data retention for cloud hosted models. Performance work is visible in the blog, with an MLX engine on Apple silicon, GGUF compatibility through llama.cpp, multi token prediction in version 0.31, and a claim of up to 90 percent faster performance with coding agents on the Aider polyglot benchmark. The cost of this convenience is control. A team that needs custom kernels, unusual quantization schemes or very specific batching behaviour may find a general purpose runtime constrains them, and the site does not claim to match specialized serving stacks on every axis.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts and the site support a picture of wide individual and team adoption rather than a claim of being the enterprise standard. The reported 8.9 million developers, the large repository following, the partnerships with OpenAI, NVIDIA and ROOST, and the integrations with Claude Code, Codex CLI and Continue all point to a tool that many people already use. It is current rather than legacy, with releases and model additions continuing into late 2026. For someone choosing what to learn, that matters: familiarity with Ollama transfers to local development, agent building and privacy sensitive deployment, and it is a reasonable default for running open models on your own machine. The site does not publish customer counts by industry, deployment sizes or job market data, so any stronger claim about enterprise dominance or hiring demand would go beyond what the material shows.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Ollama is typically used with Python and JavaScript or TypeScript applications that call its local HTTP API, and with Go, the language it is written in, for people extending it. It sits beside frameworks rather than replacing them. LangChain appears in the site's own guest post on building a retrieval augmented generation app, where LangChain handled document loading and splitting while a small Hugging Face embeddings model quantized with Transformers.js produced vectors and a WebAssembly vector store held them. Continue, Claude Code and Codex CLI are clients that speak to it. The polyglot pattern is common: a Python or TypeScript application for logic and orchestration, a Go runtime underneath for inference, and model weights pulled from a shared library. That division of labour is the point, and it means Ollama is usually one component in a stack rather than the whole of it.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about some limits and silent on others. Guest posts note that client side inference can be slower because of user hardware, and that a recommended model, Codestral 22B, carries a non production licence and heavy VRAM requirements. Cloud models are described as in preview, which signals that the hosted path is still maturing. The blog does not give detailed guidance on maximum concurrency, latency under load, or how the scheduler behaves across very large multi GPU deployments. It does not publish a formal support policy, a long term release cadence, or benchmark methodology beyond pointing to model authors' own blog posts for evaluation settings. The privacy policy is referenced for cloud models but not reproduced in the pages read. Where the material does not settle a question, such as how Ollama compares with other serving runtimes on throughput or cost at scale, the honest answer is that the official site does not say.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
